title: Fortified Wine
description: Spirit added before or after fermentation, and the families that follow.
L: Fortification means adding grape spirit to wine, raising its alcohol to 15 to 22%. The spirit is usually neutral, around 77% for Port, or around 95% elsewhere. More alcohol kills yeast and bacteria, so fortified wines are very stable and last long once opened.

Add spirit during fermentation and the yeast dies, leaving natural sugar: Port, Banyuls and Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise are made this way. Add it after the yeast has fermented the wine dry, and the wine stays dry: that's the starting point for Sherry. Some Sherries are sweetened later by blending.
How does Port keep its sweetness?
Spirit added during fermentation stops the yeast
Spirit added mid-fermentation kills the yeast, leaving natural grape sugar in the wine.

Fortification spread in the 17th and 18th centuries, when wine travelled by ship for months. Extra alcohol stopped it spoiling. British merchants shaped Port in the Douro, Sherry in Jerez and Madeira on its island. The trade explains why so many Port and Sherry houses have English names, like Taylor's, Graham's and Harveys.
Not true. Fino and Manzanilla Sherry are fortified after a dry fermentation and stay bone dry.
Fortification adds grape spirit, raising alcohol to 15 to 22%
Spirit during fermentation keeps sugar; after, the wine stays dry
It began as a way to protect wine on long voyages
Describe where Sherry is made and from what

Sherry comes from the area around Jerez de la Frontera, Sanlúcar de Barrameda and El Puerto de Santa María, in Andalusia. The main grape is Palomino, which makes a neutral, low-acid base wine. The chalky white soil, called albariza, holds water through hot, dry summers. Sweet styles use Pedro Ximénez and Moscatel.

After fermentation the wine is fortified. Wines for Fino are taken to about 15%; at this level a layer of yeast called flor grows on the surface, protecting the wine from oxygen and adding notes of bread, almonds and salt. Wines for Oloroso go to 17%, which stops flor, so they age with oxygen. Most Sherry ages in a solera, a system of barrels where young wine tops up older wine.
What does flor do to a Fino Sherry?
Protects it from oxygen and adds bready, salty notes
Flor is a layer of yeast that shields the wine from air and adds its own distinctive flavours.

A solera is a set of barrels in tiers. Wine for bottling is drawn from the oldest tier, called the solera, but never more than about a third at a time. That tier is topped up from the next oldest, called the first criadera, and so on, with new wine entering at the youngest tier. The blend keeps a steady style and gains average age.
Old tier drawn, refilled from younger
Put the solera's movements in order, starting with bottling.
Draw wine from the oldest tier
Refill it from the first criadera
Refill that from the second criadera
Add new wine to the youngest tier
Each tier passes some of its wine to the older one, so the style stays consistent year after year.
Sherry is made from Palomino on the albariza soils of Jerez
Flor protects Fino from air; Oloroso ages without it
The solera blends wines of many ages for consistency

Port comes from the Douro valley in northern Portugal, from many local grapes, led by Touriga Nacional and Touriga Franca. Fermentation is fast and intense, often by foot treading in stone tanks, called lagares, or by machines. After two or three days, at about 6 to 9% alcohol, spirit is added, leaving around 90 to 110 g/l of sugar and about 19 to 22% alcohol.

Ruby styles age briefly in large vats, keeping dark colour and fresh black fruit. Tawny styles age for years in small casks, so oxygen turns them tawny brown, with nuts, caramel and dried fruit. Aged tawnies carry an indication of age: 10, 20, 30 or 40 years old, an average style, not an exact age.
Ruby: fruit. Tawny: nuts and caramel.
Match each Port style to its character.
How a Port ages, in vat, cask or bottle, defines its style.

Vintage Port comes from a single, exceptional year, declared by each house, about three times a decade. It is bottled after two years and ages for decades in bottle, throwing a heavy sediment. Late Bottled Vintage, or LBV, is from a single year but spends 4 to 6 years in wood, so it is ready to drink sooner.
Vintage: bottle aged. LBV: wood aged longer.
Which statements about Port are true?
It comes from Portugal's Douro valley
Tawny styles age mainly in bottle
Tawny Ports age in small casks, not bottle. Vintage Port throws a sediment and needs decanting.
Port is fortified during fermentation, leaving sweetness
Ruby styles are fruity; tawnies are nutty from cask ageing
Vintage Port ages in bottle; LBV is ready earlier
Name the noble grapes and their sweetness
Explain why Madeira lasts so long

Madeira comes from the Portuguese island of the same name, in the Atlantic. On long voyages through the tropics, merchants found the wine improved with heat and movement. Today producers recreate this in two ways: estufagem, heating the wine in tanks to 45 to 50 degrees for at least three months, and canteiro, ageing in casks in warm lofts for years.
Estufagem: heated tanks. Canteiro: warm lofts.

Four noble white grapes name the main styles, from dry to sweet: Sercial, Verdelho, Boal, also spelled Bual, and Malvasia, or Malmsey. All keep striking acidity. Most Madeira, though, is made from Tinta Negra, a versatile black grape. Spirit is added during or after fermentation, depending on the sweetness wanted.
Order the noble Madeira grapes from driest to sweetest.
Sercial is the driest style, Malvasia the richest.

Madeira has already been heated and exposed to oxygen, so it is almost impossible to spoil. Bottles from the 18th and 19th centuries are still sound. Its high acidity keeps even the sweetest styles fresh. Once opened, a bottle can last for months.
Why does an open bottle of Madeira last so long?
It has already been heated and oxidised in its making
Madeira's making exposes it to heat and air, so further oxygen does little harm.
Madeira is heated by estufagem or aged by canteiro
Sercial, Verdelho, Boal and Malvasia run from dry to sweet
Heat and oxygen in its making make it nearly indestructible
Explain what a vin doux naturel is
Name the main Muscat and Grenache styles

In the south of France, sweet fortified wines are called vins doux naturels. Spirit is added during fermentation, as for Port, keeping natural sugar and reaching 15 to 18% alcohol. They are made from Muscat or Grenache, mostly in the Roussillon and the southern Rhône.
Fortified during fermentation, Muscat or Grenache

Muscat styles, like Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise and Muscat de Rivesaltes, are bottled young and fresh, with grape, orange blossom and peach aromas. Grenache styles, like Banyuls and Maury, can be fresh and fruity, called rimage, or aged with oxygen, sometimes in glass jars left in the sun, giving rancio notes of nuts and dried fruit.
Muscat fresh; Grenache can be oxidised
Which wine is a sweet fortified Grenache from the Roussillon?
Banyuls, close to the Spanish border, is a vin doux naturel made mainly from Grenache.
Banyuls and Maury are among the few wines that work with dark chocolate. Their fruit, sweetness and gentle tannin match its bitterness.
Vins doux naturels are fortified after a dry fermentation, like Fino Sherry.
Not true. The spirit goes in during fermentation, keeping the natural sweetness, as for Port.
Vins doux naturels are fortified during fermentation
Muscat styles are fresh; Grenache styles can be oxidative
Banyuls, Maury and Beaumes-de-Venise are key examples
Recognise the French sweet fortified wines
Match each wine to its region.
Each fortified family belongs to one place.
What protects Fino Sherry from oxygen during ageing?
Flor grows at around 15% alcohol and shields the wine.
Order the noble Madeira grapes from driest to sweetest.
Which wines are fortified during fermentation, keeping sweetness?
Fino is fortified after a dry fermentation.
Tawny Port gets its colour and nutty flavour from years in small casks.
Yes. Oxygen through the wood slowly turns the wine brown and adds nuts and caramel.
Spirit during fermentation keeps sugar; after it, the wine stays dry
Sherry relies on flor and the solera
Port divides into ruby and tawny families
Madeira is heated and oxidised, and lasts almost forever
